docs.title: TrustBench Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the documentation for TrustBench, a modern, framework-independent machine learning evaluation library for model reliability, robustness, uncertainty, and fairness.

Traditional model evaluation focuses almost exclusively on test accuracy. TrustBench extends evaluation to answer critical operational questions:

  • Calibration: Does the model's confidence accurately match its empirical probability of being correct?
  • Robustness: How severely does performance degrade when inputs suffer from physical, digital, or environmental corruptions?
  • Uncertainty & Error Detection: Can uncertainty metrics (predictive entropy, free energy) catch incorrect predictions before they cause failures?
  • Selective Prediction: What risk-coverage trade-off is achievable if low-confidence predictions are deferred?
  • Multi-Task & Multi-Framework: Does evaluation work seamlessly across Classification, Regression, Information Retrieval, and Semantic Segmentation across PyTorch, Scikit-learn, ONNX Runtime, and experimental adapters for Keras and JAX?

docs.title: Python API Reference
docs.text: The TrustBench Python API is organized into top-level evaluation orchestrators, protocols, task-specific pipelines, and metric modules.

docs.title: TrustBench
docs.text:
High-level orchestrator for model and dataset evaluation.

from trustbench import TrustBench

tb = TrustBench(
    model,                      # ModelAdapter, nn.Module, sklearn estimator, or ONNX session
    dataset,                    # DatasetAdapter, torch Dataset, or DataLoader
    metrics=None,               # Sequence of metric groups (default: classification, calibration, uncertainty)
    batch_size=100,             # Batch size for evaluation
    class_names=None,           # Optional list of human-readable class names
    seed=None,                  # Random seed for reproducibility
    output_dir=None,            # Optional path to persist artifacts
)

result = tb.evaluate()          # or tb.run()

docs.title: TrustBench.from_config(config_path)
docs.text:
Instantiates and configures a TrustBench instance directly from a trustbench.yaml file.

bench = TrustBench.from_config("trustbench.yaml")
result = bench.evaluate()

docs.title: evaluate(model, dataset, ...)
docs.text:
Persistence-free core evaluation function for classification models.

from trustbench import evaluate

result = evaluate(
    model,
    dataset,
    metrics=("classification", "calibration", "uncertainty"),
    batch_size=100,
    class_names=None,
    seed=42,
)

docs.title: evaluate_regression(model, dataset, ...)
docs.text:
Evaluates regression models on continuous targets.

from trustbench import evaluate_regression

result = evaluate_regression(
    model,
    dataset,
    batch_size=100,
    seed=42,
)
# Returns RegressionResult with MAE, MSE, RMSE, R², MedAE, MAPE, and interval metrics

docs.title: evaluate_retrieval(ground_truth, ranked_predictions, ...)
docs.text:
Evaluates search, ranking, and retrieval pipelines.

from trustbench import evaluate_retrieval

result = evaluate_retrieval(
    ground_truth,              # Mapping or list of relevant doc IDs
    ranked_predictions,        # Mapping or list of ranked retrieved doc IDs
    k_list=(1, 3, 5, 10),      # Cutoffs
)
# Returns RetrievalResult with MRR, MAP, Recall@K, Precision@K, nDCG@K

docs.title: evaluate_segmentation(model, dataset, ...)
docs.text:
Evaluates pixel-level semantic segmentation predictions.

from trustbench import evaluate_segmentation

result = evaluate_segmentation(
    model,
    dataset,
    num_classes=21,
    ignore_index=255,
)
# Returns SegmentationResult with mIoU, Dice, Pixel Accuracy, and FWIoU

docs.title: EvaluationResult
docs.text:
• metrics: Dictionary of computed metrics categorized by group.
  • predictions: NumPy 1D array of class predictions \((N,)\).
  • labels: NumPy 1D array of ground truth labels \((N,)\).
  • sample_ids: NumPy array of sample identifiers.
  • probabilities: Optional 2D array of class probabilities \((N, C)\).
  • logits: Optional 2D array of raw model outputs \((N, C)\).
  • summary: Dictionary shortcut to primary summary metrics.
  • save(output_dir): Atomically saves manifest.json, metadata.json, metrics.json, and predictions.npz.

docs.title: RegressionResult
docs.text:
• metrics: Dictionary of regression metrics (mae, mse, rmse, r2, etc.).
  • predictions: Continuous model predictions \((N,)\).
  • targets: Continuous ground truth targets \((N,)\).
  • residuals: Difference between targets and predictions \((y - \hat{y})\).
  • uncertainties: Optional standard deviations / confidence intervals.

docs.title: RetrievalResult
docs.text:
• metrics: Ranking metrics (mrr, map, recall@k, precision@k, ndcg@k).
  • query_ids: Identifiers for evaluated queries.
  • ground_truth: Relevant document mapping.
  • ranked_predictions: Retrieved document rankings.

docs.title: SegmentationResult
docs.text:
• metrics: Segmentation metrics (miou, dice, pixel_accuracy, fwiou, per_class_iou).
  • predictions: Pixel class masks \((N, H, W)\).
  • ground_truth: Ground truth masks \((N, H, W)\).

docs.title: Command Line Interface (CLI) Reference
docs.text: TrustBench provides a Click-powered CLI executable via trustbench.

docs.title: Commands Overview
docs.text: Command Usage Description version trustbench version Print installed package version init trustbench init [-o PATH] [--force] Scaffold a trustbench.yaml configuration validate trustbench validate [CONFIG] Check syntax and schema of configuration file evaluate trustbench evaluate [CONFIG] [OPTIONS] Execute evaluation pipeline from config report trustbench report --artifacts DIR Generate standalone HTML and JSON reports compare trustbench compare EXP_A EXP_B Compare two experiment directories

docs.title: 1. trustbench version
docs.text:
Prints the installed package version.

$ trustbench version
trustbench 0.2.0

docs.title: 2. trustbench init
docs.text:
Generates a starter configuration file with recommended evaluation defaults.

# Creates trustbench.yaml in current directory
trustbench init

# Specify custom file name
trustbench init --output custom_eval.yaml

# Overwrite existing file
trustbench init --force

docs.title: 3. trustbench validate
docs.text:
Validates model paths, dataset settings, metric groups, and reporting parameters without running inference.

$ trustbench validate trustbench.yaml
✓ trustbench.yaml is valid.

If validation fails, specific syntax or path errors are displayed with actionable hints.

docs.title: 4. trustbench evaluate
docs.text:
Executes model inference and metric computation as specified in the configuration file.

# Evaluate using default trustbench.yaml
trustbench evaluate

# Pass config path as positional argument
trustbench evaluate configs/cifar10_resnet18.yaml

# Pass config path via flag
trustbench evaluate --config configs/cifar10_resnet18.yaml

# Override output directory
trustbench evaluate trustbench.yaml --output-dir ./results/run_1

# Quiet or verbose modes
trustbench evaluate trustbench.yaml --quiet
trustbench evaluate trustbench.yaml --verbose

docs.title: Configuration Guide (trustbench.yaml)
docs.text: TrustBench uses clean YAML configuration files to define reproducible evaluation experiments.

docs.title: Configuration Specification
docs.text:
config_version: 1
experiment_name: resnet18_cifar10_evaluation
seed: 42

model:
  checkpoint_path: checkpoint/ckpt.pth  # Path to model weights
  arch_name: ResNet18                   # Architecture name
  num_classes: 10                       # Number of classes
  device: cuda:0                        # null for auto-detect, or 'cpu', 'cuda', 'cuda:0'

dataset:
  data_dir: dataset                     # Root directory of dataset
  dataset_type: cifar10                 # Dataset loader type ('cifar10', etc.)
  batch_size: 128                       # Evaluation batch size
  num_workers: 2                        # DataLoader worker processes
  split: test                           # Dataset split ('train', 'test', 'val')

metrics:
  groups:
    - classification                    # Accuracy, Macro-F1, Precision, Recall
    - calibration                       # ECE, Adaptive ECE, Brier score, NLL
    - uncertainty                       # Predictive entropy, Free energy, MSP
    - error_detection                   # AUROC, AUPRC, FPR@95%TPR
    - selective_prediction              # Risk-Coverage curves, AURC
  temperature: null                     # Optional temperature scaling factor

robustness:
  enabled: false                        # Set to true to run corruption suites
  corruption_types:
    - gaussian_noise
    - brightness
    - gaussian_blur
  severity_levels: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

reporting:
  output_dir: artifacts/experiments/resnet18_cifar10
  save_html: true                       # Generate standalone interactive HTML report
  save_json: true                       # Generate versioned machine-readable JSON

docs.title: Root Options
docs.text:
• config_version (int, required): Version of the configuration schema (current: 1).
  • experiment_name (str, required): Unique identifier or human-readable title.
  • seed (int, optional): Random seed applied to Python, NumPy, and PyTorch.

docs.title: Model Section (model)
docs.text:
• checkpoint_path (str, required): Relative or absolute path to weights.
  • arch_name (str, required): Registered model architecture name.
  • num_classes (int, required): Positive integer count of output classes.
  • device (str, optional): Target execution device (cpu, cuda, cuda:1, or null).

docs.title: Dataset Section (dataset)
docs.text:
• data_dir (str, required): Storage location of dataset files.
  • dataset_type (str, required): Dataset provider name (e.g., cifar10).
  • batch_size (int, default: 100): Batch size for batched inference.
  • num_workers (int, default: 0): Number of parallel workers for data loading.
  • split (str, default: 'test'): Split identifier.

docs.title: Reporting Section (reporting)
docs.text:
• output_dir (str, default: 'artifacts'): Destination directory for generated artifacts.
  • save_html (bool, default: true): Standalone HTML report toggle.
  • save_json (bool, default: true): Standard JSON report toggle.

docs.title: Contributing to TrustBench
docs.text: Thank you for your interest in contributing to TrustBench! We welcome contributions from researchers, engineers, and community members.

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text: This project adheres to the Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct. By participating, you are expected to uphold this code.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/Uni-Creator/trustbench.git
cd trustbench

  2. Install with development dependencies: TrustBench uses uv or standard pip/virtualenv: 

    uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e ".[all]"

  3. Verify the test suite: 

    pytest

  4. Verify linting: 

    ruff check .

  5. Build documentation locally: 

    uv run --group docs mkdocs serve

docs.title: Pull Request Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Create a topic branch: 
    git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name
  2. Keep the core small and framework-agnostic:
  3. Never import optional frameworks (torch, tensorflow, jax, onnxruntime, plotly) at top-level core modules (trustbench.core).
  4. Use dynamic imports and verify with import isolation tests.
  5. Add unit tests:
  6. Place tests under tests/unit/ or tests/integration/.
  7. Ensure pytest passes with 100% clean exit.
  8. Adhere to Code Style:
  9. Format and lint using ruff check --fix ..
  10. Update Documentation:
  11. If adding a new metric, adapter, or configuration parameter, update relevant documents in docs/ and README.md.
  12. Submit PR:
  13. Provide a clear summary of changes, rationale, and test results using the pull request template.

docs.title: Reporting Bugs
docs.text: Please use the Bug Report Template and include: - Operating system and Python version - TrustBench version (trustbench version) - Minimal reproducible example - Full stack trace

docs.title: Dataset Adapters Reference
docs.text: Dataset adapters provide a uniform slicing and indexing interface for datasets across various formats (PyTorch Datasets, NumPy memory arrays, pandas dataframes, and disk loaders).

docs.title: The DatasetAdapter Protocol
docs.text:
Defined in trustbench.core.protocols.DatasetAdapter:

class DatasetAdapter(Protocol):
    def __len__(self) -> int:
        """Total number of samples."""
        ...

    def get_batch(self, indices: list[int]) -> Any:
        """Return model inputs for the given sample indices."""
        ...

    def get_labels(self) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return labels aligned with sample order, shape (N,)."""
        ...

    def get_sample_ids(self) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return unique sample identifiers aligned with sample order, shape (N,)."""
        ...

docs.title: 1. In-Memory Adapter (InMemoryDatasetAdapter)
docs.text:
For arrays already in RAM (NumPy arrays, lists, tensors):

from trustbench.datasets.memory import InMemoryDatasetAdapter

dataset = InMemoryDatasetAdapter(
    inputs=X_test,               # Shape (N, ...)
    labels=y_test,               # Shape (N,)
    sample_ids=sample_ids,       # Optional list of identifiers
)

docs.title: 2. PyTorch Dataset Adapter (TorchDatasetAdapter)
docs.text:
Wraps any torch.utils.data.Dataset or torchvision.datasets.*:

from torchvision.datasets import CIFAR10
from trustbench.datasets.torch_dataset import TorchDatasetAdapter

torch_ds = CIFAR10(root="data/", train=False, download=True)
adapter = TorchDatasetAdapter(torch_ds)

docs.title: 3. CIFAR-10 Adapter (CIFAR10DatasetAdapter)
docs.text:
Provides standardized normalization, tensor formatting, and corruption support for CIFAR-10 evaluation:

from trustbench.datasets.cifar10 import CIFAR10DatasetAdapter, get_cifar10_datasets

trainset, testset = get_cifar10_datasets(data_dir="./data")
adapter = CIFAR10DatasetAdapter(testset)

docs.title: Experiment Management & Reproducibility
docs.text: TrustBench provides local experiment tracking, lineage recording, and reproducibility verification without requiring a hosted platform.

docs.title: Storage Backends
docs.text:
TrustBench offers two swappable storage implementations:

  1. Filesystem Storage (FilesystemExperimentStore):
  2. Zero-database dependency.

  3. Atomically organizes runs into a transparent folder structure: 

    artifacts/experiments/<experiment_id>/
├── manifest.json       # Experiment status, lifecycle, and SHA-256 hashes
├── metadata.json       # Model, dataset, environment, and hardware info
├── metrics.json        # Structured scalar evaluation metrics
├── config.json         # Exact configuration snapshot
└── predictions.npz     # Compressed NumPy arrays (predictions, targets, probabilities)

  4. SQLite Storage (SQLiteExperimentStore):

  5. Relational persistence using SQLAlchemy.
  6. Enables fast multi-experiment queries, filtering, and cross-run aggregations.

docs.title: Lineage & Provenance Tracking
docs.text: TrustBench automatically captures comprehensive lineage to guarantee reproducibility: - Model Checkpoint SHA-256: Cryptographic digest of model weight files. - Dataset Fingerprint: SHA-256 of dataset sample IDs and labels. - Random Seeds: Global seeds recorded for Python, NumPy, and PyTorch. - Environment & Hardware: Python version, OS platform, GPU driver & device name. - Execution Timestamps: ISO 8601 creation and completion timestamps.

docs.title: Verifying Integrity
docs.text:
from trustbench.storage.filesystem import FilesystemExperimentStore

store = FilesystemExperimentStore("artifacts/experiments")
checksums = store.verify_checksums("my_experiment_id")

for artifact, is_valid in checksums.items():
    print(f"{artifact}: {'VALID' if is_valid else 'CORRUPTED'}")

docs.title: Exporting & Importing Experiments
docs.text:
Experiments can be exported to standalone, portable .tar.gz archives:

# Export
archive_path = store.export("my_experiment_id", "my_experiment.tar.gz")

# Import safely with ZipSlip protection
new_record = store.import_experiment("my_experiment.tar.gz")

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text: TrustBench is designed with a lightweight, framework-independent core. You only install the dependencies required for your specific frameworks and workloads.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python: >= 3.11
  • Package Manager: pip or uv
  • OS: Linux, macOS, or Windows

docs.title: 1. Core Installation
docs.text:
To install TrustBench with base dependencies (NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-learn, Pydantic, PyYAML, Click, Jinja2):

pip install trustbench

The core installation includes complete tabular evaluation (classification, regression), evaluation engine, and CLI tools.

docs.title: 2. Optional Dependency Groups
docs.text:
Install framework and feature bundles depending on your requirements:

Extra Command Included Functionality PyTorch pip install "trustbench[pytorch]" PyTorch model adapter, torchvision datasets, GPU device transfers ONNX Runtime pip install "trustbench[onnx]" ONNX session execution (onnxruntime) on CPU or CUDA TensorFlow pip install "trustbench[tensorflow]" Keras and TensorFlow model adapters JAX pip install "trustbench[jax]" JAX/Flax functional inference adapters Storage pip install "trustbench[storage]" SQLite/PostgreSQL persistence (sqlalchemy) API pip install "trustbench[api]" FastAPI REST server and uvicorn runner Reporting pip install "trustbench[reporting]" Interactive Plotly HTML reporting and diagnostic charts Everything pip install "trustbench[all]" Installs all optional frameworks and extras

docs.title: 3. Verifying Installation
docs.text:
Verify the CLI is installed and check the version:

trustbench version
Expected output: 
trustbench 0.2.0

Verify Python imports: 

import trustbench
print(trustbench.__version__)

docs.title: Metrics Reference & Mathematical Definitions
docs.text:
TrustBench implements a comprehensive battery of evaluation metrics across classification, calibration, uncertainty estimation, selective prediction, regression, information retrieval, semantic segmentation, and algorithmic fairness.

Each metric is implemented according to published academic literature, validated against gold-standard reference implementations (such as scikit-learn, Fairlearn, and independent reference solvers), and unit-tested for edge-case safety.

docs.title: 1. Classification Metrics
docs.text: Classification evaluation assesses discrete decision accuracy and error distribution across classes.

docs.title: Definitions & Formulations
docs.text:
• Accuracy: $\(\text{Accuracy} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_i = y_i)\)$

  • Balanced Accuracy: Unweighted macro-average of recall across all classes, protecting against evaluation distortions caused by class imbalance: $\(\text{Balanced Accuracy} = \frac{1}{C} \sum_{c=1}^C \frac{\text{TP}_c}{\text{TP}_c + \text{FN}_c}\)$

  • Macro Precision, Recall, and F1: $\(\text{Macro Precision} = \frac{1}{C} \sum_{c=1}^C \frac{\text{TP}_c}{\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c}, \quad \text{Macro Recall} = \frac{1}{C} \sum_{c=1}^C \frac{\text{TP}_c}{\text{TP}_c + \text{FN}_c}\)$ $\(\text{Macro F1} = \frac{1}{C} \sum_{c=1}^C \frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision}_c \cdot \text{Recall}_c}{\text{Precision}_c + \text{Recall}_c}\)$ (Classes with zero true positives and predictions default to \(0.0\) to prevent division by zero).

  • Confusion Matrix: \(C \times C\) cross-tabulation where row \(i\) represents true class \(i\) and column \(j\) represents predicted class \(j\).

docs.title: Verification & Reference Standard
docs.text:
• Reference: sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score, precision_recall_fscore_support(average="macro"), and confusion_matrix.
  • Test Suite: Verified in tests/unit/test_metric_reference_benchmarks.py::TestClassificationReferenceBenchmarks.

docs.title: 2. Calibration Metrics
docs.text: Calibration quantifies the alignment between a model's predicted confidence probabilities and its true empirical correctness.

docs.title: Definitions & Mathematical Conventions
docs.text:
• Expected Calibration Error (ECE): Measures the expected absolute difference between confidence and accuracy across \(M\) equal-width bins: $\(\text{ECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m) \right|\)$
  • Default Bin Count: \(M = 15\) (n_bins=15).
  • Bin Partitioning: \(M\) intervals over \([0.0, 1.0]\) generated via np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, M + 1).

  • Boundary Inclusivity: Bins \(m \in \{0, \dots, M-2\}\) are left-closed and right-open \([b_m, b_{m+1})\). The final bin (\(m = M-1\)) is closed on both sides \([b_{M-1}, 1.0]\) to include predictions with exact confidence \(1.0\).

  • Adaptive Expected Calibration Error (Adaptive ECE): Addresses empty-bin and confidence-clustering artifacts by partitioning samples into \(M\) quantile bins of equal sample count: $\(\text{AdaECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m) \right|\)$

  • Default Bin Count: \(M = 15\) (n_bins=15).

  • Binning Scheme: Quantile split via np.array_split after sorting by confidence.

  • Maximum Calibration Error (MCE): Worst-case calibration gap observed across all non-empty bins: $\(\text{MCE} = \max_{m: |B_m| > 0} \left| \text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m) \right|\)$

  • Multi-Class Brier Score: Mean squared error between the full predicted probability vector and one-hot ground truth: $\(\text{BS} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{c=1}^C (p_{ic} - y_{ic})^2\)$ (Note on convention: In binary classification, this multi-class formulation yields \(2 \times\) the single-column binary Brier score \(\frac{1}{N} \sum (p_1 - y_1)^2\), accounting for both positive and negative class residuals).

  • Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL / Log-Loss): Cross-entropy loss with numerical stabilization (\(\epsilon = 10^{-15}\)): $\(\text{NLL} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ln(p_{i, y_i})\)$

docs.title: Verification & Reference Standard
docs.text:
• References:
  • Guo, C., Pleiss, G., Sun, Y., & Weinberger, K. Q. (2017). On calibration of modern neural networks. ICML.
  • Naeini, M. P., Cooper, G., & Hauskrecht, M. (2015). Obtaining well calibrated probabilities using Bayesian binning into quantiles. AAAI.
  • Ding, Y., Liu, J., Xiong, H., & Huan, J. (2020). Revisiting the evaluation of uncertainty estimation and its application to out-of-distribution detection.
  • sklearn.metrics.brier_score_loss, sklearn.metrics.log_loss.
  • Test Suite: Verified in tests/unit/test_metric_reference_benchmarks.py::TestCalibrationReferenceBenchmarks.

docs.title: 3. Uncertainty & Error Detection
docs.text: Uncertainty quantification tests whether a model's internal uncertainty signals can reliably identify incorrect predictions prior to downstream failure.

docs.title: Definitions & Conventions
docs.text:
• Predictive Shannon Entropy: Per-sample Shannon entropy: $\(H(p) = -\sum_{c=1}^C p_c \ln(p_c)\)$
  • Logarithm Base: Natural logarithm (nats), computed via np.log with a minimum probability floor \(\epsilon = 10^{-12}\).
  • Units: nats. To convert to information bits (shannons), multiply by \(\log_2(e) = \frac{1}{\ln(2)} \approx 1.4427\).

  • Range: \([0, \ln(C)]\), where \(\ln(C)\) indicates uniform uncertainty over \(C\) classes.

  • Free Energy Score: Temperature-scaled negative free energy: $\(E(x; T) = -T \cdot \ln \sum_{c=1}^C \exp\left(\frac{f_c(x)}{T}\right)\)$

  • Positive free energy \(-E(x; T)\) acts as an uncertainty score that scales with low confidence and out-of-distribution distance. Default temperature \(T = 1.0\).

  • Error Detection AUROC: Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve where prediction failure (\(\hat{y}_i \neq y_i\)) is the positive target class (\(1 = \text{error}, 0 = \text{correct}\)) and uncertainty is the decision score.

  • \(\text{AUROC} = 0.50\) represents random guessing.

  • \(\text{AUROC} = 1.0\) represents an oracle uncertainty score that perfectly flags every mistake.

  • Error Detection AUPRC: Area Under the Precision-Recall curve for error detection, sensitive to class imbalance when the base error rate is low.

  • FPR at 95% TPR: The False Positive Rate (fraction of correct predictions incorrectly flagged as uncertain) when the rejection threshold is set to capture at least 95% of all actual model errors: $\(\text{FPR}_{95} = \min \left\{ \text{FPR} \mid \text{TPR} \ge 0.95 \right\}\)$

docs.title: Verification & Reference Standard
docs.text:
• References:
  • Hendrycks, D., & Gimpel, K. (2017). A baseline for detecting misclassified and out-of-distribution examples in neural networks. ICLR.
  • Liu, W., Wang, X., Owens, J., & Li, Y. (2020). Energy-based out-of-distribution detection. NeurIPS.
  • sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score, sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_curve, sklearn.metrics.roc_curve.
  • Test Suite: Verified in tests/unit/test_metric_reference_benchmarks.py::TestErrorDetectionReferenceBenchmarks.

docs.title: 4. Selective Prediction & Risk-Coverage (AURC)
docs.text: Selective classification models have the option to abstain or defer low-confidence inferences to human experts or secondary systems.

docs.title: Coverage Range, Curve, and AURC Normalization
docs.text:
• Empirical Coverage Spectrum for AURC: The scalar metric AURC integrates across the full empirical coverage spectrum from \(k = 1\) to \(N\) (\(c \in [1/N, 1.0]\)) following the standard formulation by Geifman & El-Yaniv (2017): $\(\text{AURC} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \mathcal{R}(S_k)\)$ where \(S_k\) is the subset of the \(k\) most confident samples, and \(\mathcal{R}(S_k) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in S_k} \mathbb{I}(y_i \neq \hat{y}_i)\) is the empirical selective risk at sample threshold \(k\).

  • Optimal AURC (\(\text{AURC}^*\)): The theoretical lower bound achieved by an oracle that ranks all erroneous predictions after all correct predictions across the full dataset: $\(\text{AURC}^* = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=N-E+1}^N \left( 1 - \frac{N-E}{k} \right)\)$ where \(E = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(y_i \neq \hat{y}_i)\) is the total error count, and \(N\) is total sample count.

  • Excess AURC (E-AURC): The ranking penalty of the model's confidence scores beyond optimal ranking: $\(\text{Excess AURC} = \max(0.0, \, \text{AURC} - \text{AURC}^*)\)$ Excess AURC is lower-bounded by \(0.0\) (perfect confidence ranking) and isolates confidence ranking quality from the model's baseline error rate.

  • Discrete Risk-Coverage Table / Curve: For tabular summaries and reports, TrustBench evaluates discrete checkpoints across coverage fractions:

  • Default Checkpoints: coverages = (1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.5).
  • Customization: Any custom sequence in \((0, 1]\) can be provided (e.g. np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 20)).
  • Note: While the discrete curve summary inspects these specific coverage fractions, the scalar AURC and Excess AURC metrics always integrate over the full spectrum \(c \in [1/N, 1.0]\).

docs.title: Verification & Reference Standard
docs.text:

docs.title: 5. Regression Metrics
docs.text: Regression evaluation covers error magnitudes, goodness-of-fit, and predictive uncertainty intervals.

docs.title: Definitions & Conventions
docs.text:
• Mean Absolute Error (MAE): \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N |y_i - \hat{y}_i|\).
  • Mean Squared Error (MSE): \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\).
  • Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): \(\sqrt{\text{MSE}}\).
  • \(R^2\) Score: \(1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}\).
  • Median Absolute Error (MedAE): \(\text{median}(|y_1 - \hat{y}_1|, \dots, |y_N - \hat{y}_N|)\).
  • Maximum Error: \(\max_i |y_i - \hat{y}_i|\).
  • Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE): $\(\text{MAPE} = \frac{100}{N_{\text{nonzero}}} \sum_{i: |y_i| > 10^{-8}} \frac{|y_i - \hat{y}_i|}{|y_i|}\)$
  • Zero Denominator Handling: Samples where \(|y_i| \le 10^{-8}\) are masked out to avoid division by zero. If all targets are within \(10^{-8}\) of zero, MAPE safely returns \(0.0\).

  • Units: Expressed as a percentage (\(0 - 100\%+\)).

  • Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP) & Mean Prediction Interval Width (MPIW):

  • Requirement: Evaluated when the regression model produces sample-level predictive standard deviations \(\sigma_i\) (e.g., via predict_uncertainty, Gaussian Processes, or ensembles). Standard point regressors like Ridge do not output standard deviations; in such cases, PICP and MPIW are safely omitted.
  • 95% Confidence Interval: Formed as \([\hat{y}_i - 1.96 \sigma_i, \, \hat{y}_i + 1.96 \sigma_i]\).
  • PICP: Empirical coverage fraction \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_i - 1.96\sigma_i \le y_i \le \hat{y}_i + 1.96\sigma_i)\).
  • MPIW: Average interval breadth \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (2 \times 1.96\sigma_i) \approx \frac{3.92}{N} \sum \sigma_i\).

docs.title: 6. Information Retrieval Metrics
docs.text: Information retrieval metrics evaluate the ranking quality of retrieved documents or items for a set of queries.

docs.title: Definitions & Conventions
docs.text:
• Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR): $\(\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{|Q|} \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{\text{rank}_q}\)$ where \(\text{rank}_q\) is the position of the first relevant document for query \(q\) (or \(0\) if no relevant document was retrieved).

  • Mean Average Precision (MAP): Mean of Average Precision scores over all queries: $\(\text{AP} = \frac{1}{|R_q|} \sum_{k=1}^K P@k \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{doc}_k \in R_q)\)$

  • Recall@K & Precision@K: Fraction of relevant items retrieved within top \(K\), and fraction of top \(K\) items that are relevant.

  • Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG@K):

  • Gain Scheme: TrustBench uses linear binary gain \(\text{rel}_i = \mathbb{I}(\text{doc}_i \in R_q)\).
  • Discount: Logarithmic discount \(\log_2(i + 1)\) with 1-based rank \(i\): $\(\text{DCG}@K = \sum_{i=1}^K \frac{\text{rel}_i}{\log_2(i + 1)}\)$ $\(\text{IDCG}@K = \sum_{i=1}^{\min(K, |R_q|)} \frac{1}{\log_2(i + 1)}\)$ $\(\text{nDCG}@K = \begin{cases} \frac{\text{DCG}@K}{\text{IDCG}@K} & \text{if } \text{IDCG}@K > 0 \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

docs.title: 7. Semantic Segmentation Metrics
docs.text: Segmentation evaluation measures pixel-level classification overlap and boundary accuracy.

docs.title: Definitions & Conventions
docs.text:
• Mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU): $\(\text{IoU}_c = \frac{\text{TP}_c}{\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c + \text{FN}_c}\)$ $\(\text{mIoU} = \frac{1}{|C_{\text{present}}|} \sum_{c \in C_{\text{present}}} \text{IoU}_c\)$
  • Absent Class Handling: Any class absent from both ground truth and prediction (\(\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c + \text{FN}_c = 0\)) results in \(\text{NaN}\) and is excluded from the macro-average. If all classes are absent, mIoU returns \(0.0\).

  • Void / Boundary Filtering: An optional ignore_index parameter (e.g., 255 in Cityscapes/Pascal VOC) filters ignored pixels from evaluation prior to metric computation.

  • Dice Score (Macro F1): $\(\text{Dice}_c = \frac{2 \cdot \text{TP}_c}{2 \cdot \text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c + \text{FN}_c}\)$

  • Aggregation: TrustBench reports the unweighted macro-average across present classes (where \(2\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c + \text{FN}_c > 0\)).

  • "Mean harmonic score" denotes the macro-average of per-class harmonic means between pixel precision and recall.

  • Pixel Accuracy: Overall ratio of correctly classified pixels \(\frac{\sum \text{TP}_c}{N_{\text{valid\_pixels}}}\).

  • Frequency-Weighted IoU (FWIoU): $\(\text{FWIoU} = \sum_{c \in C_{\text{present}}} \frac{\sum_{i} \mathbb{I}(y_i = c)}{N_{\text{valid\_pixels}}} \cdot \text{IoU}_c\)$

docs.title: 8. Algorithmic Fairness Metrics
docs.text: Fairness metrics measure disparities in model predictions and error rates across sensitive demographic or operational attributes (e.g., age, gender, geographic region).

docs.title: Definitions & Zero-Denominator Safety
docs.text:
• Demographic Parity Difference (DPD): Maximum absolute difference in positive selection rate across all protected groups: $\(\text{DPD} = \max_a P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=a) - \min_a P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=a)\)$

  • Disparate Impact Ratio (DIR): Ratio between the minimum and maximum positive selection rates across groups: $\(\text{DIR} = \frac{\min_a P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=a)}{\max_a P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=a)}\)$

  • Zero-Denominator Handling: If the maximum selection rate across all groups is zero (\(\max_a \text{selection\_rate}_a \le 10^{-12}\)), TrustBench safely returns 1.0 (reflecting zero disparity, avoiding division by zero).

  • Equalized Odds Difference (EOD): Maximum disparity in True Positive Rate (TPR) or False Positive Rate (FPR) across groups: $\(\text{EOD} = \max \left( \max_{a, b} |\text{TPR}_a - \text{TPR}_b|, \, \max_{a, b} |\text{FPR}_a - \text{FPR}_b| \right)\)$

docs.title: Verification & Reference Standard
docs.text:
• References:
  • Hardt, M., Price, E., & Srebro, N. (2016). Equality of opportunity in supervised learning. NeurIPS.
  • Feldman, M., Friedler, S. A., Moeller, J., Scheidegger, C., & Venkatasubramanian, S. (2015). Certifying and removing disparate impact. KDD.
  • Matches the formal specification used by Fairlearn.
  • Test Suite: Verified in tests/unit/test_metric_reference_benchmarks.py::TestFairnessReferenceBenchmarks.

docs.title: 9. Interpretation Guide & Diagnostic Playbook
docs.text: Understanding what constitutes a "good" metric value and how metrics interact is critical for diagnosing model weaknesses.

docs.title: Diagnostic Rules of Thumb
docs.text: Metric Ideal Acceptable / Good Needs Mitigation Diagnostic Significance ECE \(0.00\) \(< 0.05\) \(> 0.15\) Low ECE means probability matches actual empirical accuracy. High ECE indicates over- or under-confidence. Brier Score (Multi-Class) \(0.00\) Task-dependent Elevated Combines accuracy and calibration in a strictly proper scoring rule. Error Detection AUROC \(1.00\) \(> 0.75\) \(< 0.60\) \(> 0.85\) allows high-confidence filtering of model failures before reaching users. FPR at 95% TPR \(0.00\) \(< 0.30\) \(> 0.50\) Percentage of correct inferences unnecessarily rejected to catch 95% of mistakes. Excess AURC \(0.00\) \(< 0.02\) \(> 0.08\) Measures gap between model confidence ranking and optimal error ranking. Demographic Parity Diff \(0.00\) \(< 0.10\) \(> 0.20\) Difference in positive rate across groups. Regulatory compliance often targets \(< 0.10\). Disparate Impact Ratio \(1.00\) \(0.80 - 1.25\) \(< 0.80\) Complies with the EEOC "four-fifths rule" when \(\ge 0.80\). nDCG@K \(1.00\) \(> 0.70\) \(< 0.50\) Evaluates ranking discount; higher indicates relevant items placed near top. PICP (Nominal 95%) \(0.95\) \(\ge 0.95\) \(< 0.90\) Empirical coverage below nominal indicates overly narrow intervals (underestimated risk).

docs.title: Metric Dynamics: Which Metrics Move Together?
docs.text:
1. Temperature Scaling:
  2. Reduces ECE and NLL without modifying logits rank order.
  3. Leaves Accuracy, Error Detection AUROC, and AURC completely unchanged because monotonic probability rescaling preserves ranking.
  4. Overconfident Neural Networks:
  5. Modern deep networks frequently exhibit high accuracy alongside poor (high) ECE and high NLL due to uncalibrated overconfidence on edge samples.
  6. Fairness vs Accuracy Trade-off:
  7. Enforcing strict demographic parity (\(\text{DPD} \to 0\)) in settings with differing base rates often slightly degrades overall accuracy or balanced accuracy.

docs.title: Example A: Classification & Calibration
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from trustbench.evaluation.calibration import compute_calibration_metrics
from trustbench.evaluation.classification import compute_classification_metrics

# Ground truth and predicted class probabilities
y_true = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1])
y_prob = np.array([
    [0.90, 0.10],
    [0.20, 0.80],
    [0.45, 0.55],
    [0.70, 0.30],
    [0.30, 0.70],
    [0.85, 0.15],
    [0.40, 0.60],  # Misclassification
    [0.10, 0.90],
])
y_pred = np.argmax(y_prob, axis=1)

clf_metrics = compute_classification_metrics(y_true, y_pred)
cal_metrics = compute_calibration_metrics(y_true, y_prob, n_bins=5)

print(f"Accuracy:    {clf_metrics['accuracy']:.2f}")     # Expected: 0.88
print(f"ECE (M=5):   {cal_metrics['ece']:.3f}")           # Calibration error
print(f"Brier Score: {cal_metrics['brier_score']:.3f}")   # Mean squared error

docs.title: Example B: Uncertainty & Error Detection
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from trustbench.evaluation.uncertainty import compute_predictive_entropy
from trustbench.evaluation.error_detection import compute_binary_detection_curve

# Compute entropy in nats from class probabilities
probs = np.array([[0.99, 0.01], [0.55, 0.45], [0.10, 0.90]])
entropy = compute_predictive_entropy(probs)  # [0.056, 0.688, 0.325] nats

# Evaluate whether entropy identifies prediction mistakes
errors = np.array([0, 1, 0])
curve = compute_binary_detection_curve(errors, entropy)
print(f"Error Detection AUROC: {curve['auroc']:.2f}")     # Expected: 1.00 (perfect separation)

docs.title: Example C: Selective Prediction (AURC)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from trustbench.evaluation.selective import compute_risk_coverage

labels = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1])
predictions = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0])  # 2 errors
confidences = np.array([0.95, 0.90, 0.85, 0.30, 0.20])

res = compute_risk_coverage(labels, predictions, confidences)
print(f"AURC:        {res['aurc']:.4f}")
print(f"Optimal AURC:{res['optimal_aurc']:.4f}")
print(f"Excess AURC: {res['excess_aurc']:.4f}")          # 0.0 indicates perfect ranking

docs.title: Example D: Algorithmic Fairness
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from trustbench.evaluation.fairness import compute_fairness_metrics

y_true = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0])
y_pred = np.array([1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0])
groups = np.array(["A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B"])

fair = compute_fairness_metrics(y_true, y_pred, groups)
print(f"Demographic Parity Diff: {fair['demographic_parity_difference']:.2f}")
print(f"Disparate Impact Ratio:  {fair['disparate_impact_ratio']:.2f}")
print(f"Equalized Odds Diff:     {fair['equalized_odds_difference']:.2f}")

docs.title: Model Adapters Reference
docs.text: Model adapters decouple the evaluation core from specific machine learning frameworks. TrustBench supports PyTorch, Scikit-learn, ONNX Runtime, Keras, JAX, and custom adapters via runtime protocols.

docs.title: The ModelAdapter Protocol
docs.text:
Any model adapter must implement the structural protocol defined in trustbench.core.protocols.ModelAdapter:

class ModelAdapter(Protocol):
    @property
    def num_classes(self) -> int:
        """Total number of output classes."""
        ...

    @property
    def supports_predict_proba(self) -> bool:
        """Whether predict_proba is implemented."""
        ...

    @property
    def supports_predict_logits(self) -> bool:
        """Whether predict_logits is implemented."""
        ...

    def predict(self, inputs: Any) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return predicted class indices (N,)."""
        ...

    def predict_proba(self, inputs: Any) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return class probabilities (N, C)."""
        ...

    def predict_logits(self, inputs: Any) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return raw unnormalized logits (N, C)."""
        ...

docs.title: 1. PyTorch (PyTorchModelAdapter)
docs.text:
Wraps any torch.nn.Module. - Automatically moves inputs to device (cpu, cuda). - Employs non-blocking asynchronous CUDA streaming (tensor.to(device, non_blocking=True)). - Executes under torch.inference_mode().

from trustbench.models.pytorch import PyTorchModelAdapter
adapter = PyTorchModelAdapter(model, num_classes=10, device="cuda")

docs.title: 2. Scikit-learn (SklearnModelAdapter)
docs.text:
Wraps any estimator supporting predict() and fit(). - Automatically discovers classes from estimator.classes_. - Handles binary, multi-class, and continuous regression estimators. - Converts decision_function to probabilities when predict_proba is absent.

from trustbench.models.sklearn import SklearnModelAdapter
adapter = SklearnModelAdapter(logistic_regression_model)

docs.title: 3. ONNX Runtime (ONNXModelAdapter)
docs.text:
Wraps an ONNX model file or pre-created onnxruntime.InferenceSession. - Works on CPU or CUDA execution providers. - Automatically discovers session input/output bindings.

from trustbench.models.onnx import ONNXModelAdapter
adapter = ONNXModelAdapter("model.onnx", num_classes=10)

docs.title: 4. Keras / TensorFlow (KerasModelAdapter) (Experimental)
docs.text:
Wraps tf.keras.Model or keras.Model instances.

[!NOTE] The Keras adapter is currently experimental. Ensure TensorFlow or Keras 3 is installed via pip install "trustbench[tensorflow]".

from trustbench.models.keras import KerasModelAdapter
adapter = KerasModelAdapter(keras_model, num_classes=10)

docs.title: 5. JAX / Flax (JAXModelAdapter) (Experimental)
docs.text:
Wraps functional models via apply_fn(params, inputs).

[!NOTE] The JAX adapter is currently experimental. Ensure JAX and Flax are installed via pip install "trustbench[jax]".

from trustbench.models.jax import JAXModelAdapter
adapter = JAXModelAdapter(apply_fn=model.apply, params=params, num_classes=10)

docs.title: Creating a Custom Adapter
docs.text:
You can implement a custom adapter by implementing the ModelAdapter protocol or subclassing trustbench.models.base.ModelAdapter:

import numpy as np
from trustbench import ModelAdapter

class ConstantModelAdapter(ModelAdapter):
    def __init__(self, constant_class: int = 0, num_classes: int = 2):
        self._class = constant_class
        self._num_classes = num_classes

    @property
    def num_classes(self) -> int:
        return self._num_classes

    def predict(self, inputs):
        return np.full(len(inputs), self._class, dtype=int)

docs.title: Plugin Development & Extensibility
docs.text: TrustBench allows external developers and teams to extend the evaluation engine without modifying TrustBench source code.

docs.title: 1. Extension Points
docs.text: You can register custom: 1. Metrics: Custom scoring functions (@register_metric). 2. Model Adapters: Custom model wrappers (@register_model_adapter). 3. Dataset Adapters: Custom data loaders (@register_dataset_adapter). 4. Input Corruptions: Domain-specific corruption functions (@register_corruption).

docs.title: Custom Metric
docs.text:
from trustbench import register_metric
import numpy as np

@register_metric("top2_accuracy")
def compute_top2_accuracy(probabilities: np.ndarray, targets: np.ndarray) -> float:
    top2 = np.argsort(probabilities, axis=1)[:, -2:]
    hits = [t in row for t, row in zip(targets, top2)]
    return float(np.mean(hits))

docs.title: Custom Model Adapter
docs.text:
from trustbench import register_model_adapter, ModelAdapter

@register_model_adapter("custom_framework")
class MyCustomFrameworkAdapter(ModelAdapter):
    def __init__(self, model):
        self.model = model

    @property
    def num_classes(self) -> int:
        return 10

    def predict(self, inputs):
        return self.model.infer(inputs)

docs.title: 3. Package Entry-Point Discovery
docs.text:
To package and distribute your plugin as an independent Python library:

In your plugin's pyproject.toml: 

[project.entry-points."trustbench.plugins"]
my_custom_plugin = "my_plugin_package:register"

In my_plugin_package/__init__.py: 

from trustbench import register_metric, register_corruption

def register():
    """TrustBench plugin entry-point hook."""
    register_metric("my_metric", my_metric_func)
    register_corruption("rain_effect", rain_corruption_func)

When TrustBench initializes, it discovers and registers installed plugins safely using Python entry points, without executing arbitrary directory scripts.

docs.title: Quickstart Guide
docs.text: Get up and running with TrustBench in 5 minutes using either the Command Line Interface (CLI) or the Python API.

docs.title: Step 1: Initialize Configuration
docs.text:
Generate a starter trustbench.yaml configuration in your project root:

trustbench init

docs.title: Step 2: Validate Configuration
docs.text:
Check that your configuration paths and parameters are valid:

trustbench validate trustbench.yaml

docs.title: Step 3: Run Evaluation
docs.text:
Execute evaluation and generate structured artifacts:

trustbench evaluate trustbench.yaml

This will run inference, compute classification, calibration, and uncertainty metrics, and output interactive HTML and machine-readable JSON reports into artifacts/.

docs.title: Basic Classification Evaluation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from trustbench import TrustBench, InMemoryDatasetAdapter

# 1. Train or load your model
X_train = np.random.randn(100, 4)
y_train = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=100)
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

# 2. Wrap evaluation dataset
X_test = np.random.randn(50, 4)
y_test = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=50)
dataset = InMemoryDatasetAdapter(inputs=X_test, labels=y_test)

# 3. Evaluate with TrustBench
bench = TrustBench(model=clf, dataset=dataset)
result = bench.evaluate()

print(f"Accuracy: {result.metrics['classification']['accuracy']:.2f}")
print(f"Brier Score: {result.metrics['calibration']['brier_score']:.4f}")

docs.title: Basic Regression Evaluation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from trustbench import evaluate_regression, InMemoryDatasetAdapter

X = np.linspace(0, 10, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
y = 2.5 * X.squeeze() + np.random.normal(0, 0.5, size=100)
reg = Ridge().fit(X, y)

dataset = InMemoryDatasetAdapter(inputs=X, labels=y)
result = evaluate_regression(reg, dataset)

print(f"MAE: {result.metrics['mae']:.3f}")
print(f"R²:  {result.metrics['r2']:.3f}")

[!NOTE] Prediction Intervals & Uncertainty (PICP / MPIW): Standard point regressors like Ridge produce scalar predictions without variance estimates, so interval metrics (picp_95, mpiw_95) are omitted. When evaluating probabilistic models (such as Gaussian Processes, deep ensembles, or custom adapters exposing predict_uncertainty(inputs)), TrustBench automatically extracts predictive standard deviations \(\sigma\) and computes 95% coverage (picp_95) and interval width (mpiw_95).

docs.title: Reporting & Visualization
docs.text: TrustBench generates both machine-readable JSON reports and standalone, interactive HTML reports viewable in any modern web browser without running a server.

docs.title: 1. Standalone HTML Reports
docs.text: Generated via trustbench evaluate or generate_html_report(): - Zero-Dependency Viewing: Fully self-contained HTML with embedded Plotly charts. Does not require TrustBench, Node.js, or an active internet connection. - Interactive Visualizations: - Confusion Matrix: Heatmap with normalized percentages and class labels. - Reliability Diagram: Expected vs observed accuracy across confidence bins with calibration gap shading. - Confidence Histogram: Frequency of predicted confidence scores. - Risk-Coverage Curve: Error rate vs fraction of retained predictions. - AUROC Curve: Error detection trade-off. - Robustness Degradation: Multi-line plot tracking accuracy degradation across severity levels.

docs.title: 2. Machine-Readable JSON Reports
docs.text:
Reports adhere to a versioned schema (REPORT_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1.0):

{
  "schema_version": "1.0",
  "generated_at": "2026-11-09T00:00:00Z",
  "metadata": {
    "experiment_name": "resnet18_cifar10",
    "model": {"name": "ResNet18", "checkpoint_sha256": "..."},
    "dataset": {"name": "cifar10", "num_samples": 10000}
  },
  "metrics": {
    "classification": {"accuracy": 0.9539, "macro_f1": 0.9539},
    "calibration": {"ece": 0.0262, "brier_score": 0.0712},
    "uncertainty": {"mean_entropy": 0.1824}
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Generating Reports Programmatically
docs.text:
from trustbench.reporting.html_report import generate_html_report
from trustbench.reporting.schema import generate_json_report

# Generate JSON
json_str = generate_json_report(result, experiment_name="run_01")

# Generate HTML
html_str = generate_html_report(result, title="ResNet18 Reliability Report")
with open("report.html", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(html_str)

docs.title: Robustness & Input Corruptions
docs.text: TrustBench benchmarks model stability under common physical, environmental, and digital input corruptions across progressive severity levels (1 to 5).

docs.title: Supported Corruptions
docs.text: Corruption Type Category Description gaussian_noise Noise Zero-mean Gaussian perturbation with escalating standard deviations shot_noise Noise Poisson noise mimicking low-light photographic sensor noise impulse_noise Noise Salt-and-pepper bit transmission dropouts gaussian_blur Blur Gaussian filtering with increasing kernel radius and sigma defocus_blur Blur Disk kernel convolution simulating optical defocusing motion_blur Blur Directional blur simulating camera or subject movement brightness Environmental Scaled pixel intensities mimicking over/underexposure contrast Environmental Dynamic range compression toward mean luminance fog Environmental Diamond-square atmospheric fog simulation jpeg_compression Digital Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) lossy block compression pixelate Digital Resolution downsampling and nearest-neighbor upscaling

docs.title: Using the Python API
docs.text:
from trustbench.robustness.evaluator import RobustnessEvaluator

evaluator = RobustnessEvaluator(
    checkpoint_path="checkpoint/ckpt.pth",
    model_name="ResNet18",
    data_dir="dataset",
    output_dir="artifacts/experiments/robustness_run",
    batch_size=128,
)

# Evaluate Gaussian noise at severity 1
metrics, predictions = evaluator.evaluate_condition("gaussian_noise", severity=1)
print(f"Accuracy: {metrics['classification']['accuracy']:.2%}")

docs.title: Using Configuration (trustbench.yaml)
docs.text:
robustness:
  enabled: true
  corruption_types:
    - gaussian_noise
    - gaussian_blur
    - brightness
  severity_levels: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Running trustbench evaluate trustbench.yaml automatically benchmarks all combinations and generates robustness degradation plots.

docs.title: Troubleshooting & FAQ
docs.text: Common questions, error resolutions, and debugging tips for TrustBench.

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'
docs.text:
Cause: TrustBench was installed without the PyTorch extra. Fix: Install PyTorch support with: 

pip install "trustbench[pytorch]"

docs.title: ImportError: ONNX Runtime is required for ONNXModelAdapter
docs.text:
Cause: The ONNX extra is missing. Fix: Install with: 

pip install "trustbench[onnx]"

docs.title: ValidationError: checkpoint_path does not exist
docs.text:
Cause: Relative paths in trustbench.yaml are resolved relative to the directory containing trustbench.yaml. Fix: Ensure your path matches the location relative to the config file: 

model:
  checkpoint_path: checkpoint/ckpt.pth

docs.title: ShapeError: Expected probabilities of shape (N, C)
docs.text: Cause: Your model's predict_proba() emitted an unexpected dimension or number of classes. Fix: Verify that num_classes matches the number of columns returned by your model.

docs.title: CUDA Out of Memory (OOM) during Evaluation
docs.text:
Fix: Reduce batch_size in your trustbench.yaml or constructor: 

dataset:
  batch_size: 64 # Reduce from 128 or 256
TrustBench uses pre-allocated memory buffers to minimize peak RAM, but GPU memory depends on model size and image resolution.

docs.title: Forcing CPU Execution
docs.text:
To evaluate on CPU even when CUDA is present: 

model:
  device: cpu
Or in Python: 
adapter = PyTorchModelAdapter(model, num_classes=10, device="cpu")

docs.title: TrustBench Example Integration Audit
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-09 Version: 0.2.0 Scope: Numerical correctness, API adherence, and regression verification across all 9 tutorial examples (examples/01_*.py through examples/09_*.py).

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
An exhaustive numerical and structural audit was conducted on TrustBench's 9 tutorial examples and their underlying evaluation modules. While all scripts were syntactically executable, the audit investigated three key numerical findings:

  1. Calibration Analysis (examples/04_analyze_calibration.py): Reached the temperature optimization boundary (\(T = 10.000\)) and previously lacked train/validation separation.
  2. Uncertainty & Error Detection (examples/05_evaluate_uncertainty.py): Observed an AUROC of 0.4835, raising questions regarding score direction and random signal behavior.
  3. Checkpoint Comparison (examples/06_compare_checkpoints.py): Printed raw dictionary keys rather than formatted metric deltas due to an argument and schema mismatch with ExperimentComparator.compare().

All root causes were diagnosed, fixed, and verified without breaking public API contracts or weakening tests. Structural and numerical assertions were added across all 9 example scripts, and 10 new regression tests were added to the test suite (tests/unit/test_example_integration_audit.py). All 204 tests pass and Ruff checks pass with zero errors.

docs.title: 1.1 Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
• Temperature Scaling Objective: fit_temperature(val_logits, val_labels) in src/trustbench/evaluation/uncertainty.py minimizes negative log-likelihood (NLL) using scipy.optimize.minimize(..., method="L-BFGS-B", bounds=[(0.01, 10.0)]).
  • Upper Bound Reached (\(T = 10.000\)): In the original example, logits were simulated as \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3^2)\) with uniform random labels. High-variance logits create extreme overconfidence (softmax probabilities approaching 1.0 even though the accuracy on random labels is only \(\approx 20\%\)). To flatten these peaky distributions and minimize NLL toward a uniform distribution, the optimizer drives \(T \to \infty\). The upper bound of 10.0 is deliberately hit as a safety ceiling. This is mathematically correct behavior for overconfident logits and is not an implementation bug.
  • Methodological Issue in Example: The original example used the exact same 200 samples to fit the temperature and compute post-calibration metrics, violating the fundamental principle of held-out calibration.

docs.title: 1.2 Fixes & Improvements
docs.text:
1. Held-Out Calibration Split: Split data into distinct calibration (150 samples) and evaluation (150 samples) subsets. Temperature is fitted strictly on the calibration set and evaluated on the evaluation set.
  2. Moderate Variance Logits + Boundary Demonstration: The primary demonstration uses realistic logits (\(\sigma = 1.5\)), demonstrating expected calibration behavior. A secondary section explicitly illustrates the high-variance boundary behavior (\(\sigma = 3.0\)), documenting why \(T = 10.0\) is reached.
  3. Assertions: Added range assertions on ECE (\([0, 1]\)), Adaptive ECE (\([0, 1]\)), Brier score (\(\ge 0\)), and temperature (\(> 0\)).

docs.title: 1.1 Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
• AUROC Value of 0.4835: The example simulated both logits and labels independently and uniformly at random. In this setting, the model predictions are uncorrelated with true labels (pure noise), and the entropy of the random softmax output provides zero predictive mutual information regarding correctness. The theoretical expected AUROC is \(0.50 \pm \text{sampling noise}\). An empirical AUROC of 0.4835 over 300 samples is within normal random deviation (\(\sigma \approx 0.035\)) and does not indicate an inverted convention.
  • Score Direction Verification: compute_binary_detection_curve(y_true_binary, uncertainty_scores) defines \(y = 1\) as errors and \(y = 0\) as correct. Higher uncertainty scores indicate higher likelihood of error. Predictive entropy \(H(p) \ge 0\) increases as probabilities become uniform (high uncertainty), which correctly aligns with the positive class (\(y = 1\)).
  • Selective Prediction & Optimal AURC: compute_optimal_aurc(n_samples, n_errors) implements the theoretical minimum risk-coverage area under perfect uncertainty ranking: $\(\text{AURC}^* = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=N-E+1}^N \left(1 - \frac{N-E}{k}\right)\)$ Verified to be monotonically increasing in error count and bounded in \([0, 1]\).

docs.title: 1.2 Fixes & Improvements
docs.text:
1. Documented Noise Behavior: Clarified in docstrings and console output that an AUROC \(\approx 0.5\) on random data is mathematically expected.
  2. Deterministic Signal Validation: Added a deterministic verification block containing 50 confident-correct samples (\(p_0 = 0.97, y = 0, \hat{y} = 0\)) and 50 uncertain-wrong samples (\(p = 0.25, y = 0, \hat{y} = 1\)). Verified that AUROC achieves \(1.0000\) and FPR@95%TPR achieves \(0.0000\).
  3. Assertions: Added assertions for AUROC bounds, non-negativity of entropy and energy, and that \(\text{AURC} \ge \text{Optimal AURC}\) (\(\text{Excess AURC} \ge 0\)).

docs.title: 3.1 Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
• API Calling Convention: ExperimentComparator.compare() signature is: compare(experiments: list[...], conditions: list[str] | None = None, ...) The example originally invoked comparator.compare(exp_a, exp_b), passing exp_b as the conditions argument rather than passing a list [exp_a, exp_b].
  • Output Schema Mismatch: compare() returns a structured dictionary:
  • experiment_ids: list of experiment identifiers
  • experiment_names: mapping of id to display name
  • checkpoints: mapping of id to checkpoint hash
  • conditions: list of evaluated conditions (e.g., ["Clean"])
  • metrics: list of metric names
  • comparison_table: nested dictionary {condition: {metric: {exp_id: value}}}
  • deltas: nested dictionary {condition: {metric: {absolute_difference, relative_percent_change, preferred}}} The example was iterating over the top-level keys (diff.items()), treating experiment_names, checkpoints, and deltas as metric groups, resulting in empty or nonsensical output.
  • Metric Grouping Convention: Scalar summary metrics must be placed under "summary" within the experiment record's metrics dictionary to be evaluated under the "Clean" condition.

docs.title: 3.2 Fixes & Improvements
docs.text:
1. Passed [exp_a, exp_b] as a list to comparator.compare().
  2. Formatted experiment inputs with metrics: {"summary": {...}}.
  3. Rewrote the display logic to cleanly format:
  4. Per-condition absolute metric values across both models.
  5. Differentials (absolute difference, relative percentage change, preferred candidate).
  6. Added assertions verifying delta computations and candidate preference direction.

docs.title: New Regression Test Suite (tests/unit/test_example_integration_audit.py)
docs.text:
10 dedicated unit tests were implemented:

  1. test_hand_computed_calibration_metrics: Hand-verified Brier score (\(0.6500\)) and Adaptive ECE (\(0.2500\)) on a 4-sample synthetic dataset.
  2. test_temperature_scaling_converges_for_well_calibrated_logits: Verified \(T \approx 1.0\) (\(0.7 < T < 1.4\)) on logits generated by a true logistic model.
  3. test_temperature_scaling_boundary_behavior: Verified safe optimization bounded at \(T \le 10.0\) without NaNs or divergence on extreme overconfident logits.
  4. test_held_out_calibration_separation: Validated calibration fitting on split A and evaluation on split B.
  5. test_perfect_error_detection_separation: Validated \(\text{AUROC} = 1.0\), \(\text{FPR@95\%TPR} = 0.0\), and \(\text{Detection Error} = 0.0\) for perfect signal.
  6. test_error_detection_against_sklearn: Verified exact parity between compute_binary_detection_curve AUROC and sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score.
  7. test_optimal_aurc_theoretical_properties: Validated boundary cases (\(E=0 \to 0, E=N \to 1\)), monotonicity, and hand calculation (\(N=4, E=2 \to 5/24 \approx 0.208333\)).
  8. test_selective_prediction_excess_risk: Verified \(\text{Excess AURC} \approx 0.0\) and \(\text{AURC} = \text{Optimal AURC}\) under optimal uncertainty ranking.
  9. test_checkpoint_comparison_schema_and_deltas: Validated schema, relative percentage change, and metric optimization direction (accuracy \(\to\) higher preferred; ece \(\to\) lower preferred).
  10. test_checkpoint_comparison_empty_and_single: Verified graceful handling of empty lists and single-experiment comparisons.

docs.title: Known Limitations & Methodological Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Synthetic vs. Real-World Calibration: In synthetic experiments with random targets, temperature scaling will typically drive toward the maximum bound to minimize cross-entropy loss against high-entropy labels. When evaluating real models (e.g., ResNet on CIFAR-10), temperatures typically calibrate in the range \(T \in [1.1, 2.5]\).
  2. Error Detection on Uninformative Representations: AUROC measures the ranking capability of uncertainty scores relative to misclassifications. If a model's predictive entropy is uninformative regarding its failure modes, AUROC will be near \(0.50\). Users should evaluate multiple uncertainty metrics (MSP, Entropy, Energy, MC Dropout) to identify the best discriminator for their specific task.
  3. Experiment Comparison Input Format: ExperimentComparator.compare() expects a list of experiment dictionaries or ExperimentRecord objects. Scalar metrics should be nested under "summary" for baseline comparison or under condition keys (e.g. corruption names) for multi-condition comparison.

docs.title: TrustBench Release Audit — Initial Architecture & Codebase Assessment
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-09 Version Evaluated: 0.2.0 Status: Mandatory Pre-Cleanup Assessment (No modifications performed prior to this inventory)

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
TrustBench is designed as a lightweight, scikit-learn-like library and CLI for machine learning model evaluation (reliability, robustness, calibration, uncertainty, and performance).

This initial audit evaluated all source code files, configurations, dependencies, documentation, examples, and packaging outputs. The audit identified key areas where the codebase can be cleaned up, simplified, and hardened for production release: 1. Dependency Inconsistencies & Phantom Extras: The pydantic-settings dependency is declared in core dependencies but never imported. The dashboard optional dependency extra declares streamlit>=1.66.1, but there is zero Streamlit or dashboard code in the entire repository. Core dependencies declare excessively strict minimum versions matching the development environment (e.g. numpy>=2.4.6, scikit-learn>=1.9.1, torch>=2.14.1). 2. Optional Dependency Leakage: Eager import torch in trustbench/datasets/__init__.py (via torch_dataset.py) and trustbench/models/__init__.py (via 17 PyTorch CIFAR-10 model architecture files) causes non-PyTorch imports (e.g., from trustbench.datasets import InMemoryDatasetAdapter or from trustbench.models import SklearnModelAdapter) to fail when PyTorch is not installed. 3. Compatibility Shims & Duplication: Five redundant 10–15 line compatibility shims exist (trustbench.data.cifar10, trustbench.evaluation.artifacts, trustbench.evaluation.reproducibility, trustbench.evaluation.inference, trustbench.robustness.report). 4. Legacy PyTorch Model Clutter: 17 CIFAR-10 model architecture files in src/trustbench/models/ contain copy-pasted if __name__ == '__main__': test() blocks and eager torch imports. 5. Storage / API Coupling: fastapi and uvicorn are bundled under [project.optional-dependencies].storage, coupling database persistence to web server packages.

docs.title: TrustBench Release Readiness Report
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-09 Version: 0.2.0 Release Readiness Decision: READY FOR RELEASE

docs.title: 1. Executive Assessment
docs.text:
Following an extensive audit, architectural decoupling, dependency pruning, and validation across clean virtual environments, TrustBench v0.2.0 satisfies all production readiness gates and is classified as READY FOR RELEASE.

The library achieves: - A scikit-learn-like, lightweight public Python API (TrustBench(model=..., dataset=..., metrics=[...]).evaluate()). - Pure NumPy-based core evaluation that operates cleanly without PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, or Streamlit. - Strict optional dependency isolation: importing core dataset or model adapters does not load deep learning frameworks or web servers. - Fully working Click-based CLI (init, validate, evaluate, inspect, compare, version). - 204 automated tests passing in 7.08s. - Zero Ruff linting or code quality errors. - Verified isolated installation and end-to-end evaluation from both wheel (.whl) and source distribution (.tar.gz). - Complete documentation and 9 end-to-end verified tutorial examples.

docs.title: 2. Architecture & Public API Assessment
docs.text:
TrustBench maintains a modular, decoupled architecture:

[Public API & CLI]
        │
        ▼
[Core Evaluation Engine (pure NumPy)] ◄───► [Protocols: ModelAdapter / DatasetAdapter]
        │                                                     ▲
        ▼                                                     │
[Task Evaluators & Metrics]                       [Framework Adapters (lazy)]
  - Classification, Calibration, Uncertainty        - PyTorch (nn.Module)
  - Regression, Retrieval, Segmentation             - Scikit-learn (estimator)
  - Fairness, Distribution Shift, Streaming         - ONNX Runtime (InferenceSession)
        │                                           - Keras / TensorFlow
        ▼                                           - JAX / Flax
[Persistence & Reporting]
  - Atomic Filesystem Store (JSON / NPZ)
  - Optional SQLite / SQLAlchemy Store
  - Standalone HTML & Plotly Visualizations

docs.title: Public API Compatibility
docs.text: All public imports advertised in documentation and trustbench/__init__.py remain intact and backward compatible: - from trustbench import TrustBench, evaluate - from trustbench import ModelAdapter, DatasetAdapter - from trustbench import PyTorchModelAdapter, SklearnModelAdapter, ONNXModelAdapter, KerasModelAdapter, JAXModelAdapter - from trustbench import EvaluationResult, RegressionResult, RetrievalResult, SegmentationResult - from trustbench import register_metric, register_model_adapter, register_dataset_adapter, register_corruption

docs.title: 3. Code Cleanup Summary
docs.text:
1. Dependency Pruning:
  2. Removed unused pydantic-settings from core dependencies.
  3. Removed phantom dashboard optional extra (streamlit>=1.66.1), eliminating 16 unused transitive dependencies from the lockfile.
  4. Decoupled storage (sqlalchemy>=2.0.0) from api (fastapi>=0.100.0, uvicorn>=0.20.0).
  5. Relaxed overly strict pinned minimum versions in pyproject.toml (numpy>=1.24.0, scipy>=1.10.0, scikit-learn>=1.3.0, torch>=2.0.0, torchvision>=0.15.0) to avoid rejecting valid user environments.
  6. Removed duplicate jinja2 and pillow declarations from optional extras.
  7. Framework Isolation:
  8. In src/trustbench/models/__init__.py: Replaced 17 eager PyTorch CIFAR-10 model imports with an on-demand __getattr__ dynamic loader. As a result, importing trustbench.models or SklearnModelAdapter no longer loads PyTorch into sys.modules.
  9. In src/trustbench/datasets/__init__.py: Made TorchDatasetAdapter lazy-loaded via __getattr__, allowing InMemoryDatasetAdapter to be used in environments without PyTorch.
  10. Dead Code Elimination:
  11. Removed legacy src/trustbench/data/ package (cifar10.py), updating scripts/train_baseline.py to canonical trustbench.datasets.cifar10.
  12. Removed dead def test(): ... and if __name__ == '__main__': routines across 16 CIFAR-10 model architecture files.

1. Synthetic Data Calibration Boundaries: When fitting temperature scaling on high-variance synthetic logits (\(\sigma = 3.0\)) with random targets, temperature optimization will reach the safety upper bound (\(T = 10.0\)). This is mathematically expected behavior for overconfident logits.
  2. Optional Framework Dependencies: Users evaluating PyTorch, ONNX, Keras, or JAX models must install the respective extra (trustbench[pytorch], trustbench[onnx], etc.) or install the framework into their environment.
  3. Release Blockers: None.
